utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. And just before we call the witness, a very minor half decision; it's not a full one. On the 13th of October, 2006, the Defence filed a motion for admission of the statement of Witness MM-084 pursuant to Rule 92 ter. In its oral response on the 19th of October, 2006, the Prosecution did not object to the admission of the statement under Rule 92 ter. The Trial Chamber considers that the statement of the witness will fulfil the requirements of Rule 92 ter if on the day of the witness's testimony the witness is present in court, available for cross-examination, and any questions by the Judges, and attests that the written statement accurately reflects his declaration and what he would say if examined. Therefore, the Trial Chamber finds that upon the fulfilment of these conditions, the statement of Witness MM-084 will be admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter. Thank you. Any other housekeeping? You promised not to have any housekeeping until the 20th of November, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'm sticking with my pledge, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. May the witness please be brought into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. May I remind you once again that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- you are -- thank you. That you had are bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions now about arming. You testified on Wednesday that Martin Spegelj concluded an agreement in October of 1990 with Hungary worth, you say, $192 million to purchase 60.000 to 80.000 Kalashnikovs, but yesterday, sir, you testified that by January 1991 Croatia had imported only 30.000 weapons. So can you tell me which of these two stories that you have given the Trial Chamber is true.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both versions are true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The import of arms, on the basis of resources paid in, was carried out in success, successively and not in one fell swoop. There was a lengthy period of the importation of weapons from Hungary into the territory of the Republic of Croatia with which the troops of the Republic of Croatia were armed. According to available data in 1991, there had been 30.000 Kalashnikovs, I suppose perhaps even more. But another fact is that there is still a dispute being conducted between Croatia and Hungary for failure to pull -- pay in the full amount of the resources for the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So in fact, your testimony is that by January of 1991 Croatia, you say, had imported some 30.000 weapons?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the information that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, sir. Now, isn't it true, in fact, that United States intelligence estimated that in January of 1991 -- and maybe you would -- maybe you don't know this - if you don't, just say - that the Croats had sufficient arms to arm only approximately 10.000 men? Isn't that, in fact, true, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our figures are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And isn't it also true that the biggest -- the biggest arms deal that Martin Spegelj ever concluded was for 30.000 weapons, not 60.000 weapons, and that in fact he never received most of those weapons. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How, then, did Croatia have in 1993 150.000 troops and their arms and in 1995 200.000 soldiers bearing arms --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this is the figures that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to suggest that that's -- that that's not responsive to my question. If you could just really focus on my question. My question was: Isn't it true that in -- that the big deal that you're talking about was really for no more than 30.000 weapons and that most of those weapons were never received by Martin Spegelj. Isn't -- and if you disagree, just say so, please.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree, and I have given an answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, that's fine --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- some of the weapons paid for were never delivered to Croatia, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you; that's very helpful. Thank you, sir. Now, are you aware that in August of 1991 Martin Spegelj was dismissed by Mr. Tudjman from the government; do you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlacic, he used to be the minister first, and after that he was the commander of the National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Isn't it true that he was dismissed from the government in August of 1991. He later came back as an advisor, but in August of 1991 he was dismissed from his position in the government. That's true, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're not aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he held the office of minister of defence; after that, he was an advisor; following which he was the first commander of the National Guards Corps. And then the Main Staff was formed, the Chief of Staff, the first one was Bobetko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did he stop being minister of defence; do you know?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know it to be August -- approximately August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are insisting on it. I am telling you I cannot tell you the exact time. I know the time when he was the commander of the National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking for the exact time now. I'm asking for an approximate time. Was it approximately August of 1991, or are you unable even to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was about that time, but I'm not sure about the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now, let's talk about the other side with respect to arming. Are you aware, sir, that Milan Martic and others in the Krajina began arming the Serbs from approximately August of 1990 on?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Milan Martic did that and that the Serbs were being armed in that period. I know that we as the army followed in parallel both the situation and the arming of the Serbian population. And of the Croatian population, and I can give you several facts, if you wish, about the arming of the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let me put a few questions to you. It started in the fall of 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometime -- it began sometime around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And -- and, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 19th of August on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's the 19th of August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The MUP of Serbia was involved in the arming of Serbs in the Krajina in 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified that the arming of Croats was unlawful and illegal. Those were the words that you used. Was the arming of Serbs in the Krajina also unlawful and illegal?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time arming was carried out by legalising the procurement of weapons by the authorities having legalised the procurement of weapons, and people bought their weapons from trading organisations. They also took arms from memorial museums. And according to our information, there had been some weapons hidden from the previous war and that was the way in which the proposition armed themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, sir, are you telling us that the arming of the Serbs was done legally?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see that they were organised -- that there was organised arming. That it was organised from a different foreign state namely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I really urge you to listen to my question carefully. I wasn't asking you if it was organised or if it was from a foreign state. Question -- you described the arming of the Croats as illegal and unlawful. Are you saying that the arming of the Serbs in the Krajina that started after the 19th of August, 1990, was legal?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the legislation in force, it was illegal in certain places.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. It was illegal in the same way that you say that the arming of the Croats was illegal; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I answer that yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And at the time the JNA believed that it was illegal, that the arming of the Serbs in the Krajina in 1990 was illegal. That was what the JNA thought; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you testified about disarming -- the order to disarm in January of 1991. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware that Milan Martic promised to return weapons but that in fact he did not do so? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm perfectly aware of what Milan Martic said, and I said in my statement that weapons which were taken by the police from the police station in Knin, which was around a hundred rifles, were returned to the commission. So from that particular police station, all the 100 rifles were returned to the commission which had been set up by the Yugoslav People's Army, which commission worked in the northern barracks. There were also three light machine-guns, and I cannot give you the exact figures but there were several tents of long-barrelled weapons which the people returned. People, as I told you, armed themselves either by taking weapons from museums or different ways, so procurement --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you're going beyond really what the question is about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did he actually begin to get into the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He's gotten into part of it, because he responded to the first part which is what Martic promised to return and then talked about some weapons. So I'm going to pursue this, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't see where he said that Martic promised anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, he said, "I'm perfectly aware of what Milan Martic said," and he doesn't say what he said. That's correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question -- the answer to the question should be: Yes, I'm aware; or, no, I'm not aware. Any lengthier answer than that is not the answer. The question was: Are you aware that Milan Martic promised to return weapons but that in fact he did not do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Martic promised to return the weapons and he did return them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, may I -- thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you're not telling us -- you're not going to tell us that all the weapons that had been obtained illegally during -- starting after August 1990 were returned in January of 1991 and amounted to a hundred rifles and some light machine -- three light machine-guns and so forth. Those were not all the weapons that had been illegally obtained, were they?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The data that was available to us was that from the police station the police, or the militia as we call it, in Knin had taken out 100 rifles and three light machine-guns from that station and those were returned to the commission that had been established. I'm not aware whether any other weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, wait a minute, wait a minute. The weapons that you're talking about that were taken from the police station were actually taken on the 17th of August, 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th or on the 19th. Actually, I think it was on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you told us just a moment ago that starting on the 19th of August, 1990, there was illegal arming of Serbs in the Krajina. Now, would you agree with me that the weapons that were received in the Krajina illegally by Serbs after August 19th, 1990, were not returned in January of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asseverate that according to our information what the policemen had taken out they returned --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and another portion of the weapons was returned --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's put aside the weapons that the policemen took out. Let's just put that aside for a moment, okay? There were -- the other weapons that were received in the Krajina illegally in 1990 were not returned; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that for you. But a part of the weapons which were held by the population, apart from the weapons that were taken from the police station, was also returned. I also know that there were profiteers who sold the weapons there to the peasants.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, the -- I take it that the Federal Secretariat of Defence and Veljko Kadijevic had access to the same information you had, if not more than you did; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to look, please, at a -- at a page of Borislav Jovic's book. Are you familiar with his book?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll still look at it. It's the entry for the 9th of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 476, and the English it's -- we want to look at page 038; and in the B/C/S we're going to start at 039. And I hope that's clear. I think it will be clear when ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And as it's coming up, the -- the entry for the 9th of January, 1991, in Borislav Jovic's book discusses a report that was submitted to the SFRY Presidency on -- and discussed by the Presidency by the -- by the Federal Secretariat of National Defence. And the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down to the bottom of that -- of the B/C/S page, please. The English went up on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That will be fixed in a moment. Now, I think it's about halfway in that paragraph it talks about -- it says -- and on the English it's the -- it's almost at the end of the first paragraph there where it says: "The report goes on to discuss the self-organisation of Serbs in Krajina. In the territory of Knin Krajina armed groups have been formed for which weapons are being acquired in various illegal ways. In that region, there are several thousand rifles and pistols of various types and even some hand-held rocket-launchers" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Whiting, I'm a bit lost. I'm not sure I'm with you. My English page is headed "preface." Page 38, eh? Sorry, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see that, Witness, sir, Mr. -- do you see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm with you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where I'm reading from?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can be of assistance to my friend, Mr. Whiting, we have 242, and maybe now something's just come up. The page we have is 242 in the B/C/S, and the subject matter discussed there is entirely different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is about the arming of the Croats by the Croatian authority --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There you go. The Mostine warehouse and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try and move to the next page then. Is this -- should be -- I can't see it, but is it -- it should be 039 or 040. Is that right? This is -- we're now in 040? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see now the discussion of the arming of the Serbs in the Krajina, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have activities of the Croatian authorities against the JNA, and then it talks about Serbs self-organising in the Krajina. In the Krajina area armed groups were set up, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's it. That's exactly what I'm looking for. And it talks about -- do you see it talks about several thousand rifles and pistols and hand-held rocket-launchers and explosives? It also in the next paragraph talks about the armed people of Serbia --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that, I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you just read about the self-organisation of Serbs in the Krajina. Keep reading to the end of that paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And do you see in the next paragraph it talks about the armed people of Serb nationality have been organised into armed structures --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, is it because it goes on to the next page?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next paragraph it says: "The armed people of Serb nationality have been organised into armed structures and staffs for use on specific communication" -- Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- so those weapons, those several thousand rifles and pistols, were not returned on -- in January 1991, were they? Because your testimony is that it was some hundred -- maybe a hundred rifles or a hundred weapons.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, I was only talking about Knin itself. I wasn't talking about the entire area covered by the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which included, I think, a total of 28 municipalities, such as Knin. I wasn't really in charge myself. There were various JNA units organising this, operative units, in charge of Lika, Kordun, Banja, Western Slavonia, Eastern Slavonia, and commissions were set up in those areas; therefore, I don't know how many weapons were seized in those respective areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's go back to the paragraph that the Prosecutor first read. That paragraph says: "The report goes on to discuss the self-organisation of Serbs in Krajina." And then it says: "In the territory of Knin Krajina, armed groups have been formed for which weapons are being acquired in various illegal ways. In that region, Knin Krajina, there are several thousand rifles and pistols of various types and even some hand-held rocket-launchers." So the figures given here are with respect to Knin. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Knin is not the Serbian Krajina. Knin is a near municipality within the Serbian Krajina. Knin is a small place in relation to the Republic of Serbian Krajina as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know, sir, and that is not the point of the question. The point of the question is that this document is telling us of the number of arms and ammunition that were circulated in Knin. It says "Knin Krajina," so they're talking about the Knin area, that part of the Krajina that's called Knin, there were several thousand rifles, unless I'm misunderstanding the statement. The writer here specifically refers us to Knin, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reference here is to the Knin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, the -- what does that mean, what does "Knin Krajina" mean? You tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Knin Krajina includes the general area of northern Dalmatia, Lika, Kordun, and Banja. These are four different areas that at the time were absorbed into the Knin Krajina. I'm telling you about Knin itself, and I can hardly be expected to talk about something that the then-president Jovic may had written about. Maybe he had more information than I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. If Knin Krajina means that whole area, then I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you don't really think that there were no more than a hundred rifles in the Knin area, do you, and that those were all returned in January 1991? You don't believe that, do you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, you didn't allow me to answer. We knew that the population was being armed by certain profiteers, if I may call them that, who were selling weapons to these people. And these peasants, the population, would have to give a cow in order to get a single carbine and that there were weapons that had been legalised at an earlier stage, or at least I assume so. But those weapons, the hunting weapons, and everything else, the licenced weapons, those were never seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So your testimony is that there were only a hundred illegal weapons in the Knin area in January 1991, and that they were all returned. Is that really your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our information, that was our military information. There weren't many weapons around. I am telling you, each village had between 10 and 15 hunters which each owned a rifle or a carbine or something like that, and those were licenced weapons with proper certificates, which means if you add up all these weapons the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I think you've answered the question. You know, don't you, that in January of 1991, at least by then, weapons were being brought from Belgrade to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, if we could look at Exhibit 501, please, and if we could look at page 1 of the B/C/S, and page -- well, first, let's -- page 1 of the B/C/S and page 1 of the English. This is a report from a JNA security organ dated the 23rd of January, 1991, about information received from a source. And if we could scroll down on the bottom of the B/C/S and turn to page 3 of the English, please. It says -- it says: "In the next few days trailer trucks carrying about 37.000 pieces of weapons are expected to arrive from Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you not aware of this information in January of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, this is the security organ of the 5th Corps of the air force and anti-aircraft defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, please --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and their headquarters was at Bihac. This has nothing whatsoever to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The question is: Were you aware of it in January 1991 or not, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information could be reliable or unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's true also, sir, about the information that you've shared with this Tribunal about Croatian arming, correct, it could be reliable or it could be unreliable? In fact, that's true about all the intelligence and facts and things that we heard that you testified about. Isn't that right? It could be reliable or unreliable?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that is true. I worked with the security organs, and let me tell you something. There is a degree of reliability, reliable, unreliable. As for any information provided by the state or any of the state organs, well, that is usually founded on hard facts. As for Croatian information, I have a document on me now and I might as well hand it to you for you to see how many weapons were coming into Croatia at the time. The federal government at one point decided to step in in order to stop the weapon influx.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So what you're telling me is that the information that you have about Croatian arming is reliable, but information about arming of the Serbs is not reliable, or possibly is not reliable. That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not what I said. Rather, I said: Information provided by security organs is usually classified as not probable, quite probable, or little probable; that's how they're classified. If you can give that document back to me, I can perhaps check the classification of that document for you and see what it says. This is not an original document produced by a security organ --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This header is definitely not their official header.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this document's in evidence so that -- sir, so the document can be considered by the Trial Chamber in light of your testimony. However, the information that you provided about Croatian arming is -- it's all the same type of information, right, it's from sources and information that's been gathered. It's the same kind of information, isn't it, sir? You didn't see 60.000 weapons or 30.000 weapons being bought by the Croats, did you? It's all from intelligence information.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I'm telling you, I am in possession of an official document of the federal government about the arming of the Croats. I think the document has been admitted. I'm not sure if it's available now, but it certainly was delivered to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. By -- you know, sir, don't you, that by March or April of 1991 a training camp was established in Golubic where special purpose units of the SAO Krajina police were trained and armed, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a training camp in Golubic, but I don't think those were armed special units of the police. Because in order to arm a special unit member, in order to train them, it takes over a year. You can't have a 20-day course, such as the one run by Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you a question. Let's maybe back up a little bit. Was Golubic in your area of responsibility at the time, in March/April 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, it wasn't within my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. So you don't really know that -- what was going on at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, I had information that indicate to Captain Dragan had organised training for men for a month, so that they would learn to use weapons in order to set up barricades and protect the Serb population from any attacks by the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How -- sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also know this --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question before you tell us that. How far away is Golubic from your area of responsibility, how many kilometres?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My command was in Knin itself, the barracks in the north; and Golubic is some distance away --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's about --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it must be about 7 or 8, perhaps up to 10 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, so then you -- you certainly would have an interest in knowing what's happening, what kind of military or police or whatever kind of training is going on 7 to 10 kilometres away from your area of responsibility, right? That would be something important for you to know?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know that, Mr. Prosecutor, I did know that. I even know how many --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter couldn't catch the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The last part of the answer, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know how many --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of the answer. The interpreter didn't catch that. You knew you said ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew what was going on in Golubic. I knew how many men were being trained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know that the men who were being trained there were -- became members of special units of the SAO Krajina police? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that some 80 to 100 people were trained there in different groups. It is probable that a part of the trainees later entered those units, but we cannot speak about special units because a member who has completed special training, which takes over a year, can join the special police units, not this particular training which only lasted one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm only using the language that they used. The -- within the SAO Krajina police there were what were called special purpose units, right? There was one, in fact, in Knin. And there was one in Benkovac, and there was one in Plaski. You know about that, right, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the special police units, we had the special police units, the PJM, which was not the special police -- the special purpose police --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm talking about 1991. Let's focus on March of 1991. Don't move to 1992. Let's focus on March of 1991. There were special -- just yes or no. Do you know if there were -- that there were special purpose units within the SAO Krajina police; for example, in Knin, in Plaski, in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There only existed the police of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you're not aware of special purpose units in existence in Knin, Benkovac, Plaski, you don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Not in a single document is there a reference to the existence of special purpose police units but only the militia or the police of the SAO Krajina. And the special police units were set up only as of the 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 they were organised, these special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you sure you had good intelligence about what was happening in -- around Knin in March of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that the training camp at Golubic was under -- was within the Ministry of the Interior and was under the command of Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that camp was in operation from around the 5th of March, if I recall it exactly, up until June when the then-current president of the SAO Krajina, Mr. Milan Babic, actually told Mr. Dragan that he had over -- Captain Dragan that he had overstayed his welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time men were trained to man barricades --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, sir, you've told us some of those things already, and -- but none of those things are an answer to my question. My question was: You know, don't you, that the training camp at Golubic was within the Ministry of the Interior and was under the command of Milan Martic. Do you know that or don't you? We're talking about March of 1991.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about those relations, whether he was under the Ministry of the Interior or under the Territorial Defence of the Krajina is something I can't say with --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You didn't know that --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- precision because those relationships -- I'm telling you that I know that there was a camp, that training was being conducted there, and the training was delivered by Captain Dragan. He actually made statements to the effect of how many people were trained, in what time-periods, et cetera, and that confirmed our own information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, really, please focus on my question. I know you're -- I know you're understanding my questions, so please try to focus on them and answer my questions. And if you don't understand my question, just tell me and I'll rephrase it, okay? Now, you described the National Guards Corps in Croatia as a paramilitary formation. Whatever these units were that were being trained at Golubic, they were also a paramilitary formation; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally and legally observed, they were paraunits, and I know that in fact they used a third of their men in order to counter the Yugoslav People's Army in any attempt to disband them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is there a difference between paramilitary formation and paraunits?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paraunits can be paramilitary and parapolice. When you say "paramilitary," that refers exclusively to the military organisation of such paraunits.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move on to another subject. You testified that Croatia "officially proclaimed the JNA to be hostile on the 23rd of March, 1991." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not what I stated. I said that the -- that Croatia declared the JNA to be hostile, not that the JNA was -- had a hostile attitude to Croatia. On the 23rd of March, Croatia stated --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I think there may have been a mistranslation there, and maybe it's because I was speaking too quickly, and I'll put the question again. You testified -- or rather, let me say it again. You testified that Croatia: "Officially proclaimed the JNA to be hostile on the 23rd of March, 1991."

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you give us the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The reference is 9694, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'm glad I was prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before I ask you about that, I want to ask you about some other things that were happening in March of 1991. You're aware, are you not, that on the 15th of March, 1991, the SFRY Presidency met and refused a request from the JNA to declare a state of emergency. You know about that, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you know also that the representative from Serbia on the SFRY Presidency, Borislav Jovic, immediately resigned from the Presidency, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you know, don't you, that on the 16th of March, 1991, Slobodan Milosevic made a speech in which he said: "Yugoslavia has entered the last phase of its agony." Are you aware of that speech?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, do you know that in that --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't ring any bells.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, does this ring a bell that he said that the Republic of Serbia, in that same speech, would not recognise any decision reached by the SFRY Presidency because it considered its decisions illegitimate. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's watch the speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could switch to the Sanction, please. This is Exhibit V0002155 but we'll watch it on the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Having seen the speech of the 16th of March, 1991, of Slobodan Milosevic, do you now remember it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I remember it. That was extracted from its context, I mean before, and I see that the president of Serbia realistically assessed the situation and estimated the state of affairs in the state realistically, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you saw that he said that the -- Yugoslavia has entered the last phase of its agony, right? You saw that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the president of the Presidency came to Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you also saw that he said that the Republic of Serbia would not recognise any decision reached by the SFRY Presidency, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency was not complete, and the president of the Presidency was seeking to dismember Yugoslavia, which he confirmed when he arrived in Zagreb and said, "I have completed my task; Yugoslavia is no more." Mr. Mesic --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, who was the president of the Presidency in March of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and after that Mr. Kostic assumed the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mesic was not the president of the Presidency because he was blocked from becoming the president. Isn't that true? He only became the president in June of 1991.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he actually assumed the duty of president of the Presidency and continued to work on a break-up of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He assumed the Presidency in June of 1991. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And by the way, the -- just so we're clear, the Presidency of the SFRY has command over the JNA, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency as the -- as a collective body was the Supreme Command of the Yugoslav People's Army, under the constitution and law.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And let's go back now to what you say happened on the 23rd of March, 1991. But before I do that, I forgot to ask you something. You were interviewed by members of the Defence for Milan Martic sometime before January of 2005, right? So some years ago.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was a little confusing; I agree. Let me make it clearer. You were first interviewed by the Defence for Milan Martic sometime before January of 2005, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was sometime in 2004 that I talked with Mr. Nikolic, the investigator concerning the -- this defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I take it that aside from some minor details, everything that you've told us in your testimony here you told Mr. Nikolic back in 2004; correct? I had a number of talks, a number of interviews after that as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt a little bit. I don't know whether the rest of the people have the message that I have on my screen about "Kadirah smoke." There's a message here that says it's from Pertak, or somebody, to Registry on the 20th of October, 2006, 3:13:30, and then it's talking about smoke. We shouldn't burn inside here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It just popped out on its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: May I proceed while it's being attended to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, while we burn, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If anyone smells smoke, I'm sure that we'll hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, when -- when you had this -- you met them first -- you met Mr. Nikolic back in 2004, and when did you have subsequent meetings with him?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't be very specific about when. We met several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four or five other meetings, official interviews, in his office. And we met about twice, about town, to discuss some things --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before I arrived here, I was in touch with him three times about my passport, about travel arrangements, that sort of thing. He took out my visa and took care of everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm interested in the substance. When would you say -- by when would you say you had provided Mr. Nikolic with all of the information that you have provided the Trial Chamber here in your testimony? Was it by 2005 or was it earlier this year? When would you say that was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I informed him about that during our first meetings back in 2004. I had all of that written down, and when I was telling him about things he made his own selection as to what would or would not be included in the eventual statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So if I've understood you correctly, everything you've told us here in the past couple of days you told Mr. Nikolic back in 2004?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there is a record to show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. Let's go back to the 23rd of March, 1991. Who do you say declared the JNA hostile? You said it was -- Croatia officially declared it. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatian territory suddenly there were leaflets says "death to the JNA." If you require a copy, I have some on me and you could perhaps tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That same day I learned from the military intelligence -- military security service --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This leaflet, did you provide this leaflet to the Defence or did you tell them about it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, for some reason they've chosen not to submit it. But the leaflet, does it -- is it from the Croatian government, or does it say who it's from?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leaflet said that it was the Croatian government and the Croatian people declaring the JNA to be hostile. That same day official documents arrived in all police stations that the name of the JNA would have henceforth not be officially used any longer. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) They received this information, and he informed the security organ of the 9th Corps that the army was now being thrown out of official use, that the manpower of the police in Croatia should be raised by 10 per cent. These are excerpts from that particular order dated that particular day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we go back to an earlier question which, according to me, hasn't been answered. At page 27, line 16 to 18, you asked the question,

utterances.speaker: MR. PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: "Is it from the Croatian government, or does it say who it's from?" I don't think that question has been answered, notwithstanding the lengthy explanation that was given in response. And I'm interested in an answer to that question. Is this leaflet, does it -- does it come from the government of Croatia; and if not, where does it come from? Who do you say it comes from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian government officially took that decision on the 23rd of March --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Immediately there was this leaflet that emerged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. I'm asking you a simple and straightforward question. Did that leaflet -- was it produced by the government of Croatia or does it state who it is from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the government adopted the decision to reject the JNA from any form of official use in Croatia, and then suddenly this leaflet was being distributed throughout Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about any decision of the government. I'm just asking you about the leaflet. I'm asking you if this leaflet was generated by the government of Croatia; and if it's not, does it state who it is from and who is that? That's all I'm asking you. I'm not asking you about decisions of other people. Please listen to the question and focus on the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hardly know who wrote the leaflet, whether it was a government official or someone like that. I do know that the leaflet suddenly turned up all over the place, in the countryside, in the cities. It was dropped in JNA mail. I have a copy of that, and if you want to see one, I have it on me. I'd be glad to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I don't want to see it. You don't know whom it is from. That's your answer. You said: "I can hardly know who wrote the leaflet." So you don't know who wrote the leaflet; that's your answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we might be talking at cross-purposes. What I said is I do know that the government took that decision. I do not know who physically produced that leaflet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for the clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge Hoepfel was drawing my attention to something that I saw from the corner of my eye that a security officer was passing on a note to the Defence counsel. May I suggest, Mr. Martic, in line with what we discussed yesterday that we shouldn't cross our lines with the rules of the security, and that if you have anything just raise your hand and the Bench will ask Mr. Milovancevic or Mr. Perovic to come to you. Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, would you please go and attend to Mr. Martic. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's put aside -- sir, let's put aside the issue of the leaflet, because you've told us now about that. But you have insisted a number of times that Croatia -- that there was some decision that was made by the Croatian government. Can you be more specific? Who made the decision? What did the decision say? Did you see the decision? How did you know about it? Could you tell us though things, please.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was through the Croatian public media; more specifically, the Croatian Radio Television. They announced that such a decision had been made, which we found very disquieting. And suddenly all over barracks and towns in Croatia this leaflet started turning up, and that's also what I told you about the document which emerged in the Drnis police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, please -- okay. Let's take this one part -- step at a time. You said it was in the Croatian media. I take it that if it was on the radio and television, it was also in the print media?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we didn't have Croatian newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you since -- since that time in 2004 or 2005 or 2006, have you seen any articles from that time about this order or decision from the Croatian media?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't read the Croatian print media.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But has anyone shown you in -- for example, in your interviews with the Defence, your various meetings with Mr. Nikolic, did he ever show you any kind of an article from the Croatian media about this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did the decision actually say? What decision -- what did the decision say that the Croatian government took?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can tell you is what the leaflet says. I can read that back for you, if you like. As for the decision, I can hardly be expected to repeat the decision verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I don't need it repeated verbatim, and I really -- I don't want to hear any more about the leaflet. That's focus on the decision, and it doesn't need to be verbatim. What did it say? Not verbatim, just generally what did it say? And by the -- who made the decision? Was it the Assembly? The president? Or who -- where did the decision come from?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian leadership took a decision, quite literally, for the JNA to be ejected from any form of official use in the Republic of Croatia, saying something to the effect that the JNA was now buried and no longer existed for the Republic of Croatia or its people. That is the essence or a summary, if you like, of that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, when you say the Croatian leadership, what do you mean specifically, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian leadership includes the government; the parliament as the upper-most legislative body; and atop of them all, the president of the Republic of Croatia, President Franjo Tudjman, who was also the supreme commander of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you're saying this decision was taken by all of those people, by the parliament, and the president, and so forth? They together made this decision?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about technicalities, and I'm telling you about this decision and what I know is based on media reports, TV reports, Croatian Radio Television, which we were still watching in Knin at the time. They took this decision. I'm not sure how they took it in purely technical terms. I wasn't there, and I didn't see this being done for myself. I was never in the Croatian parliament or at any of the government meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This was obviously a public decision, right? This wasn't a secret decision. This was public, wasn't it, according to you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a public decision since it was in the public media. It was publicly announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why didn't you get --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I listened to this TV announcer announcing that the Croatian leadership had taken such and such a decision. That's precisely that they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And didn't you get -- go and get a copy of the decision, since it was public and since it concerned the JNA, which you were a member of? Weren't you interested in seeing actually the decision itself?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't technically possible for us to obtain a copy of this decision from the Croatian government or their leaders. Everything we knew came through the public media at the time, but we did find this leaflet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- I'm going to interrupt you because you've answered my question and I've gone over the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it's a convenient time. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that on the 2nd of May, 1991, some residents of Zadar gathered after a funeral and demolished some shops and buildings belonging to Serbs. And this is sometimes referred to, I think, as crystal night in Zadar; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: He didn't use the word some hundred --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I think he said something like a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, that's correct, Your Honour. I think it was -- right, there is a figure. That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in fact what happened on that day -- what happened on the 2nd of May, 1991, is that before this happened, before these events happened in Zadar, is there was a clash in Borovo Selo in which 12 Croatian policemen were killed and another 20 injured, and in fact there were stories that the bodies of the Croatian policemen had been mutilated. Isn't that what occurred on the 2nd of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the figures. As for something happening in Borovo Naselje, yes, there were clashes between members of the Croatian MUP and groups of armed locals in Borovo Selo. I don't know about the exact figures in terms of casualties on either side --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, if it wasn't --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as for what happened in Zadar --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you talked about Zadar, you talked about one person -- a funeral for one person. But -- maybe you don't know whether it was 12 or 11 or 13, but it was approximately that number, correct, of Croatian policemen who were killed at Borovo Selo, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the distance between Borovo Selo and Knin must be over 400 kilometres, if my reckoning is correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the time and the distance --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, the question is: That happened -- those number of men were killed, those number of policemen, approximately 12 policemen were killed at Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, 1991; correct? You know that.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you're saying, that 12 policemen were killed. I am telling you that people were killed on both sides --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but I can't give you a figure. I'm under oath. Was it 5, 6, 12, 20, I really don't know. I do know that there were casualties on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was more than one Croatian policemen, wasn't it, sir; you know that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, well, then it must be. Certainly there was more than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's what you -- I want -- I want to know what you know. If you don't know, just tell me. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the witness has given two answers here. I'm not quite sure which one he wants the Court to accept. He says: "If you say so, well then it must be." That's the one answer. The other answer is: "Certainly there was more than one," in the same answer. Now, "certainly there was more than one," is his answer. The first part is what he says is your answer. Now, question to you, Witness, is: Which one shall we accept? Is it: Certainly there was more than one? Do you know that for a fact? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were casualties on both sides; that must be more than one. That must be several at least, but I can't give you an exact figure. I'm under oath, and I can't afford to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm not asking you to speculate. I'm just asking you to say whether it's more than one and you have answered me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's perfectly all right to say you don't know if you don't know the answer to a question. Now, what happened, then, in Zadar on the evening of May the 2nd, 1991, is that a large crowd gathered to protest and -- these events that had occurred in Borovo Selo and the crowd became violent. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said, and this has nothing to do with Borovo Selo. In my evidence I said as follows: On that day --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a member of the Croatian MUP named Franko Lisica was buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There's no need to repeat your evidence. We actually have it all written down and we know what your evidence was. If you disagree with what I say, you can simply say: I disagree. So you disagree that the crowd on -- in Zadar on May 2nd, 1991, had gathered because of the events at Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And -- thank you --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because of the death of this Croatian police officer named Lisica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did that Croatian police officer die at Borovo Selo, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Borovo Selo, at least as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And would you agree that the crowd that -- that gathered that night became violent. It became out of control and became violent in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that when you have a crowd, a crowd always tends to lose control and act in all sorts of irrational ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this crowd lost control and became violent in Zadar; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, the crowd had been assembled at the request of the leaders of the Croatian Democratic Party, the Croatian Democratic Union in Zadar, the local branch, and then they got out of control and did what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir -- thank you. They got out of control. Thank you. And one of the reasons they got out of control was because of what happened that day to the Croatian policemen in Borovo Selo. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that one. I don't associate that with Borovo Selo. These are two different areas --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But they happened --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I simply can't possibly draw any logical parallels between these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you don't know. The answer is you don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But isn't that question already answered?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I had asked it with respect to gathering and I was asking it with respect to getting violent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You asked earlier, Mr. Whiting, that the crowd in Zadar on that day gathered to protest against the death in Borovo Selo. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. And his answer -- he disagreed and said that it was because of the funeral and then also added that it was organised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So in that event, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, this funeral, you asked if this can be linked to Borovo Selo and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. And he said no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- isn't Borovo Selo is quite in a different region as the witness wanted to say. Isn't this -- is this Borovo Selo -- Witness, if I ask you, is this near Vukovar, is that this one, Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the immediate vicinity of Vukovar. It is in the eastern part, the separated part of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... place sounds a little strange that this should be then the funeral in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I didn't think it was. I didn't think it was, and the witness said that it wasn't a funeral connected to the -- it would also be strange that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It was just a question that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was a question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Just to be clear -- now let me check to say if I need to ask this question. Okay. So you don't -- you don't know if one of the reasons the crowd became violent in Zadar on the night of May 2nd, 1991, is because of what had happened in Borovo Selo that day? You don't know whether that's true or not?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I do know what the real cause was and I have said that. I don't want to repeat it, unless you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, that answer is sufficient. Thank you. Now, you testified also about a speech that Mr. Tudjman made in Trogir on the 5th of May, 1991. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And isn't it true that in that speech the only thing that Mr. Tudjman -- or let's say, at most Mr. -- what Mr. Tudjman said was that people should protest -- mount protests outside of barracks of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not so. Tudjman issued precise instructions, a task, to be carried out to block the JNA barracks and to prevent deliveries of food and other necessities to JNA barracks. And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look, please, at an exhibit, 06046499.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this is a document that I have only in English, so I'm going to have to read you the relevant portion. It's very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, I forgot to ask that the last speech from Mr. Milosevic be admitted into evidence, given a number. It's V0002155, and we have the clip and also a transcript in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought when you asked for it you called it an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I shouldn't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You shouldn't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I don't recall if I did, but if I did, I should not have. It's not an admitted exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, it was a little funny to me because the numbering was not according to the numbering of exhibits. But anyway, be that as it may, that clip showing a speech of the late Slobodan Milosevic is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. And what else?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, there's a transcript that goes with it. It can be given one number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Together with the transcript thereof.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit Number 979.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, was there a certain reason you said the last speech of Mr. Milosevic. The speech we saw last?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's what I meant. I'm not being very clear today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It certainly wasn't his last speech; that's for sure. Now, if we could look at this article. This is an article from the Guardian newspaper dated the 7th of May, 1991, and it contains information from Tanjug.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'll just read to you it's the paragraph that starts: "Quoting unspecified news reports." It says: "Quoting unspecified news reports, the ministry implied that the President Franjo Tudjman had incited the incident" -- and this appears from the article to be a reference to the Ministry of Defence of the SFRY which is referenced in the first paragraph. "It claimed that during a speech on Sunday in nearby Trogir he asked why people had not demonstrated outside army buildings." Now, it doesn't say anything about precise -- giving precise instructions to blockade the barracks or cut off food and water or anything, it's just talking about demonstrating. Isn't that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to have the entire text translated into the Serbian language, and then I could be in a position to make a proper comment. But let me say if you consider an article by the Guardian a document, it is quite a different thing what was talked about at the political gathering of the leadership in Dalmatia. What Tudjman actually issued is not always made public. You must allow for that possibility. We know what followed --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, sir, my question -- my question to you was about the speech that he made. Okay? So let's keep our focus on the speech. And with respect to the rest of this article, only that paragraph is about the speech. Isn't it true what it says in that article that what he said in the speech was about demonstrating at the barracks; he didn't make -- give any instructions to blockade the barracks or anything like that in May of 1991.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We summarised that demonstrations, protests, and assemblies of people can assume a negative course, and these gatherings in Zadar did assume a negative course with an onslaught on the barracks ensuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, what you're saying is that Tudjman called for demonstrations but these demonstrations took on a negative character. Is that a fair characterisation of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said that such demonstrations could have taken on a negative course with the barracks being targeted. For example --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on the 6th of May in Split --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, let's stop. Let's keep our focus on the speech. You accept that the speech --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think Mr. Martic has a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You accept, sir, that the speech --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Colleague Whiting. Your Honour, Mr. Martic asked me a while ago that he was not in breach of order, but when he tried to actually get my attention in order to pass me the note, the guard sitting by him thought that it was normal for the guard to actually pass, because this is what is done in other cases. So this is all I wanted to say, and I do apologise for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. We also did not suggest that Mr. Martic was in breach of the order. We understand, and we understand the difficulty, and we're trying to be as helpful as we possibly can. Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, you accept, though, that in the speech by Mr. Tudjman he spoke about demonstrations; correct? That's what he spoke about in the speech at Trogir on the 5th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree completely, because after that speech there were practical actions. Sasa Gesovski -- Sasa Gesovski, a soldier in our command, was killed on the 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever actually seen the speech or seen a transcript of the speech?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not have seen the -- or obtained the, rather, transcript of that speech in any way. We could only have had information by way of intelligence gathering or what was being said and then we could observe for ourselves what happened in the field in Dalmatia. I tell you, on the 6th of May this soldier was killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, you've told us about the 6th of May. This was a public speech, was it not? I mean, people could hear this speech; it's reported in a newspaper.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to say that the newspapers do not always carry everything that is being talked about and agreed at such political gatherings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was it a public speech?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tudjman actually had a working meeting with the leadership of the Dalmatia region with the representatives of the Croatian Democratic Union --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you. Answer my question: Was it -- to your knowledge, was it a public speech? The speech that you talked about it, was it a public, or was it a secret speech?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the speech --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm talking about the speech --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I'm talking about the meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm asking about the speech. Please answer my question. Was it a public speech or a secret speech or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held in a public place. There was no need for it to be held in a secret place, and what he issued for the public was also in a public place, not in a secret place. Trogir is a public place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. So -- but you're telling us that you were unable to -- the JNA was unable to obtain an accurate report of what that speech was or what -- or a copy of the speech or a video of the speech or -- you had to rely on intelligence to find out what was said in that speech?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had intelligence data. And if you would like me to tell you, on the 6th of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
