utterances.text: -- the commander of the Military Naval District was in person at my command post --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, no, what I'd like you to do is answer my question, please. Are you telling us that the JNA was unable to obtain a copy -- reliable, accurate information about a public speech given by Mr. Tudjman in Trogir, either from the media or a transcript of it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA was capable of obtaining such data and extracts of that data through -- and I did get extracts from the data through the command and control and information system. And some of the facts were confirmed for me in person by the commander of the Naval District who was, on the 6th of May, at my command post and who had then learned that his soldier had been killed. He did not finish the scheduled inspection tour, and he then flew there by helicopter to Split, and this was Admiral Mile Kandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, would you not, sir, that if Mr. Tudjman had really made a public speech on the 5th of May, 1991, giving specific instructions about blockading JNA barracks, that would be big news. That would be something widely reported and a big event in May of 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The blockade of the Military Naval District followed immediately the -- on the next day --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- also attacks on some attacks on the village of Sibenik ensued on the next day --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, please, this will really -- this will take a long time if you don't focus on my question and answer my question. My question was: A speech of that nature, what you have described his speech to be, that is specific instructions to blockade JNA barracks, that would be big news in May of 1991 and widely reported; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you the answer that you expect to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The answer I expect is just an answer. So if you could just answer the question either way.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained to you that what I have in front of me and what you have read out for me is an excerpt from the papers, and what we had and what was agreed at the meeting I've already explained. What was agreed were blockades of barracks and other measures, cutting off electricity and water-supply and telephone lines --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- And I explained what happened the next day --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I can just have a moment. I asked you -- it's at page 39 of our transcript. I asked you about the speech that Mr. Tudjman made. And you said -- and I asked you -- I asked -- I put to you that he only talked about protests. And you said: "That is not so. Tudjman issued precise instructions, tasks, to be carried out to block the JNA barracks and to prevent deliveries of food and other necessities to JNA barracks." That was your testimony, sir. Now my question is, and please listen to my question --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That would be big news at that time. In May of 1991, that would be big news if Mr. Tudjman was -- in a speech at Trogir making -- giving instructions, specific instructions, to block the JNA barracks. That would be big news and widely reported; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time Tudjman did not issue any public orders through the mass media. I am telling you that I got this information from the commander of the Military Naval District, who came on the next day to inspect the 9th Corps, and it is from him that I learned that. He confirmed that what I said was so and what -- the events that followed actually bore that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So what you're telling us is that -- because in June of 1991 Mr. Mesic assumed the Presidency of the -- the presidency of the Presidency of the SFRY, and you're telling us that even -- which has command over the JNA, and yet in May, a month before that, you're telling us that Tudjman is issuing orders and instructions to blockade the barracks? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this article be admitted into evidence and given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The article is admitted into evidence. May it please be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 980.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, sir, the truth is that the blockades that you have talked about again and again in your testimony did not begin until late August or September of 1991, right? With the exception -- with the exception of a few barracks in Western Slavonia near the border of Hungary that were attacked in July of 1991. Isn't that true? Isn't that the truth, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand the second part of your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the former, I can tell you this --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let me try and put the whole question to you. The truth is that in July of 1991 there were a few barracks attacked in Western Slavonia, but that the other barracks were not blockaded until August -- end of -- late August or September 1991. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This applied to all JNA barracks in Croatia. Measures started being implemented in May, citizens assembling, cutting off the barracks, electricity and water-supply and phone lines. As for a specific order that was given to attack the barracks, this was issued on the 15th of September, 1991, by the president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, in person --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me put it this way --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: The blockade -- the barracks were not blockaded in Croatia until the end of August or September of 1991. Let's put aside some individual attacks that may have occurred. The barracks were not blockaded until the end of August or September of 1991, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many were --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- their food supply was cut off -- for example, if you take the Rogoznica barracks --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, hang on. Let's just try to move forward. You know that Mr. Kadijevic, Veljko Kadijevic, wrote a book called "My View of the Breakup."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Whiting, what does "many were" mean? Many were before the relevant date or many were not. The question that you asked at 48, line 16 -- 15 onwards, the answer is "many were" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I may have heard more of that answer than was recorded, so -- but I can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you -- the question I put to you is that, in fact, aside from some individual attacks that may have occurred on barracks, the barracks were not blockaded until the end of August or September of 1991. And can you answer that question briefly.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many barracks that had been blocked before that date in different ways with their supplies, regular supplies, being cut off. For example, the Rogoznica barracks. Instead of supplies of flour and bread being delivered, members of the Croatian MUP sent canned dog food in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But the -- the -- okay. Let's go to my next question. You are aware, are you not, that Mr. Kadijevic wrote a book about the events in 1990/1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, Mr. Kadijevic was your superior officer in the JNA at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kadijevic was the federal minister of All People's Defence at the time. My direct superior was the corps commander. At the time - I think you're asking about 1991 - there was a succession of three different corps commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But I wasn't asking about your direct superior. He is the -- he is the guy in charge of the JNA; correct? Mr. Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the federal minister of All People's Defence, and he was a member of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Have you read his book?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Portions of it. Some excerpts were published in our newspapers, so I read those.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could -- we have portions in evidence, and if we could look at Exhibit 24, please. And I want to look at page 70 of the English version, which is at 011, ERN, and then page 129 of the B/C/S, which is at -10 ERN. And if you could scroll down on the B/C/S version and move it over to the other side. It's page -- there we go. And on the English version I'm looking at the paragraph that begins: "Therefore Croatia," and do you see -- it's the paragraph that begins at the bottom there. And it says -- Mr. Kadijevic says: "Attacks on military units and garrisons in Croatia began at the end of the summer in 1991, although by the end of July barricades were already being raised against the garrisons in Virovitica, Krizevci, Bjelovar, and elsewhere, along with other acts of provocation. This marked the beginning of the second phase of armed conflict in Croatia, which lasted until the Vance Peace Plan was accepted."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, what Mr. Kadijevic writes in his book is true, isn't it, that the attacks on the barricades began at the end of the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirmed this in my testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes, and I confirmed about the individual cases as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could look at -- very briefly at an ECMM document dated the 7th of January, 1992, it's Exhibit 00230700 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. And this one is admitted, so it doesn't need to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. And if we could go to page 3. This -- I don't believe there's a B/C/S of this -- I'm sorry, it's -- if we could go three more pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Here --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was good, down, if we could scroll down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I apologise for this being in English and I'll just read for you what it says. This is an ECMM report which is about -- it's written on the 7th of January, 1992 -- or, rather, it's about -- I apologise. It's about a JNA air force attack on ECMM helicopters that occurred on the 7th of January, 1992, and it contains some information. And it says in paragraph 11 in the last sentence it says: "Later, again for reasons of safety, during the blockade by the Croatians of the Yugoslavian National Army barracks which began on 14 September 1991, all three ECMM helicopters were moved ..." And you would agree with that, would you not, sir, what's written there, that the blockade by the Croatians began on the 14th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started attacking the barracks on the 14th, the preliminary stage assembling; and then on the 15th there was an all-out attack that was launched on all the JNA barracks throughout Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit Number 981.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you just a couple of questions about the nature of the blockades or barricades on the barracks. They did not completely immobilise the JNA or prevent the JNA from functioning, right, because the JNA was able to engage in offensive actions during the fall of 1991, even after the barricades had started; correct? For example, in Drnis, in Sibenik, Saborsko, Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, neither Skabrnja nor Saborsko were barracks. But in Croatian territory each and every JNA barracks was blocked and attacked, except for the following: Benkovac, Knin, Petrinje, those were the ones that were not blocked or attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So my -- the question that I'm putting to you is that -- even once the barricades started on the 15th of September, 1991, the JNA could still function and mount offensive attacks; correct? The JNA wasn't completely immobilised, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA in Montenegro, Macedonia and Serbia, for example, the barracks there were not blocked at that time, and it was in those areas that -- could continue to work under peacetime conditions, so to speak. However, those in Slovenia or in Croatia were entirely blocked off. Croatia, for example, each and every JNA barracks in Croatia was fully blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, you accept, do you not, that the JNA was nonetheless able to mount offensive actions after the 15th of September, 1991. You have testified about some of them, Drnis, Sibenik, other places in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA had the ability to carry out short operations in certain areas in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. Okay. Thank you. That's really what I was asking. Now, sir, in your long experience as a military man, I take it you have had training and become familiar with the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You would agree with me, then, I take it, that JNA barracks, garrisons, are a legitimate military target in a war; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aggressor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you mean by: "The aggressor, yes." Let's assume there is a war going on in Croatia, attacking -- barricading JNA barracks is -- that is a legitimate -- and just thinking only about the laws of war, that's a legitimate military target; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the JNA barracks in Croatia at the time could in no way have been conceived as a legitimate target for Croat paramilitary units. At the time, Croatia was still part of Yugoslavia's constitution; it was part of Yugoslavia constitutionally, and it had every duty to act in keeping with the constitutional provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you're -- I'm not talking about the Yugoslav constitution or the laws in Yugoslavia. I'm just talking about the laws of war, the international laws of war. Put aside whether the conflict was legitimate or not. Under the laws of war, a military barracks -- barricading a military barracks, that's a legitimate military target; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're talking about at cross-purposes here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have two countries at war. If you have two countries at war, then a military barracks becomes a legitimate target. For example, there is a war between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro, then a Bosnian barracks in Montenegro would have constituted a legitimate target.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example. But under these conditions, the conditions that prevailed at the time, there is no way that the JNA military barracks could possibly be construed as having been a legitimate target.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But that's only because in your view the JNA was the only legitimate army in the former Yugoslavia at the time, and the Croatian paramilitaries had no right to exist. That's really what you mean, right, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, under the constitution, under all the existing laws at the time, the JNA, until the 19th of May, 1992, remained the only legitimate military force in the SFRY, which includes Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to ask a question here for my own education because I know very little about laws of war. If the war is a civil war, would -- would it be legitimate to barricade a military installation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm no lawyer myself. I don't think that is envisaged by that particular law. It's very difficult to answer that one, to be quite honest. This was more about a war of secession, which also bore some features that resembled a civil war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you a very simple and straightforward question. In a civil war, now like in Darfur, for instance, where members of the same country are fighting, would it be legitimate for the combatants to attack military installations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that question with any disagree of precision. I simply can't because I personally wasn't preparing for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, Your Honour, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, in fact, in the summer of 1991 the JNA was mounting attacks on Croatian forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The summer of 1991 the JNA was repelling attacks launched by Croat paramilitary forces. They were not mounting attacks; they were repelling attacks and trying to lift the siege of their own barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking now about the time before the siege of the barracks --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But if we could look at a document. It's 03 -- in English, the English number is 03004214. It has a different B/C/S number, which I can provide if that's helpful. This is -- if we could make it so the whole page could be visible in the B/C/S. This is a document which is dated the 25th of July, 1991, and it's a protest, a strong protest, by the government of the Republic of Croatia to the SFRY Presidency. And if you could just -- if we could just scroll down and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did -- are you familiar with this document? Was this something that you saw in your capacity --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never set eyes on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this is a document produced by the 9th Corps at all, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, you're right about that. Now, do you see -- it says in the first paragraph, it talks about on the 25th of July the JNA opened artillery and tank fire in Erdut and Bogojevci?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is written here. But never having set eyes on this document, I cannot confirm its authenticity, nor could I have known anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about its authenticity. I'm just asking you to comment on what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in the B/C/S and in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, to be fair, most of the things that are talked about here are in Eastern Slavonia, which is outside your area and -- but perhaps things that you may have heard about, would have been relevant to you, in terms of the conflict in Croatia. And did you hear about any of these things that are listed here? For example, in point 1 the JNA plane machine-gunning a silo in Eastern Slavonia? Number --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it is illusory for me to discuss this document because this concerns a completely different strategic group. This is the command of the 1st Military District and I was in the Military Naval District. These are huge territorial distances. So I am unable to confirm this either way. I see a piece of paper, there is something written on it, but I cannot discuss those facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, in points 2 and 3 there are -- talk about JNA attacks that occurred in the Banja region, which is certainly close -- not so far from your area. Now, I take it that these are things that even though they're not in your area, because they concerned the conflict between the JNA and Croatian forces, these are things you would be informed about, no?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as regards Banja, that is within the competence of the 2nd Military District. It was. And these are some minor things here that I should not have been informed about nor did I know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 982.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at another document, please. This is a -- the English is 00501213.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And as this document's coming up on the screen, sir, you know that on the 5th of August, 1991, there was a cease-fire declared in Croatia; correct? And in fact, I think it may have been the SFRY Presidency that declared it, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- some 14 cease-fires had been declared --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- perhaps one was declared also at that time. I cannot recall that exactly. I know that -- about the cease-fires that were declared on the territory of the Naval District on the 25th of September, namely --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, please, this is really going to take a long time. Please just focus on my question. My question was about the 5th of August, 1991. We've had evidence about this in our case. Are you unaware of the cease-fire that was declared on that day?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact dates of the numerous cease-fires. We can assume -- I can accept that for a fact that a cease-fire was also declared on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, this document is a chronology of attacks that had occurred since the cease-fire had come into force until the -- and it was written, this document, on the 7th of August. And it says, according to this document, and that -- that 107 heavy armed terrorist attacks, three of which being instigated by the armed formation of Yugoslav army have been committed until the present day, and ten members of the MUP and ZNG were killed and 42 wounded. And then the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- goes through and lists various attacks that occurred, including, in the beginning there, in your area in Northern Dalmatia and Lika. Are you familiar with those events that occurred on those dates?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have known nothing about the existence of a place called Bela Gorice in the area of Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we turn to the next page, please, if you just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not in my zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Some of these events are in your zone, though, right? Benkovac --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Benkovac never was in my zone of responsibility. It was the Sinj-Knin and Drnis-Knin axis that were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know anything about these events that were occurring just outside your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to these which we can see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about these events. I know of these places. I don't know anything about those events, if they did occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, this is Lika, this is also outside the zone. This is Plitvice, Otocac, that was not even comprised within the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 983.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djukic, you testified about the ethnic composition of the JNA and you testified that it -- in -- it changed in the latter part of 1991. That's at 9687. Now, this was a process that occurred over time, correct, it didn't just happen on one day?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This process unfolded more intensively from the first half of 1991, as of June, namely, and gained -- and actually developed intensively until the pull-out of the JNA from the territories of Slovenia and Croatia. I have figures for this period that I'm referring to; namely, that about 12.000 active officers and non-commissioned officers left the JNA and about 7.000 civilians working in the army, of which 62 per cent were Croats and 16 -- about 16 per cent were Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, some of the Serb officers were forced into early retirement; correct -- I mean some of the non-Serb officers were forced into early retirement; correct? In other words, they didn't leave voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the figures that I indicated, some of the officers, both Croatian and Serbian, were retired early or, according to the law, when they fulfilled legal conditions. One portion of them deserted and some of them asked to be removed from active military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that by September of 1991 all of the Military District and corps commanders were either Serbs or Montenegrins?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't give you a precise answer. I know about those who were in the territory of the Military Naval District and the command of the Knin Corps --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the Knin -- commander of the Knin Corps --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- those who were at the level of the strategic formations --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The commander of the Knin Corps from the summer of 1991 on, that is, the commander of the 9th Corps from at least the summer of 1991 on, was a Serb, it was Spiro Ninkovic, then Vladimir Vukovic, then Ratko Mladic, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as of the 16th of June, 1991, until the 16th of September, 1991, the commander of the Knin Corps was Spiro Ninkovic, a Montenegrin, who hailed from Bar, the Republic of Montenegro. And from the 16th of September up until the end of January 1992, it was General Vlado, or Vladimir, Vukovic, who was a Serb. And then for a short stint, up until April, it was General Ratko Mladic, who was replaced until the 19th of May by General Savo Kovacevic, all of them Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask a question out of curiosity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It may not -- it's not relevant at all. What was the normal retirement age in the army, in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The retirement age in the JNA, the standard age or the period of pensionable service was 40 years of service, which did not correspond to the effective time of service but was also something which was creditable to personnel in the JNA. So an officer in the JNA would be credited a year and a half for a year of service, and some other services, like the border services or other services. Had 18 months. So according to the law on the JNA, one could retire with -- after 30 years of service; and according to such a provision, I actually was retired having completed 33 years of active service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you were asked on direct examination what other forces, apart from JNA forces, participated in combat operations of the 9th Corps in the second part of 1991, specifically in Sibenik, Drnis, Kijevo, and others. And your -- you answered: The Territorial Defence, the TO. But aren't you forgetting something, forgetting someone else -- another armed force that participated?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there were no other armed forces in the area of the 9th Corps, apart from the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, what about the police? Aren't you forgetting the police?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police does not constitute armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an instrument of civilian authority serving to maintain and restore law and order and discharge other duties, as envisaged under the law. We did not have a state of war to be able to recruit police for such purposes, nor did we have a declared state of emergency. There was no declaration of any such states by the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The police -- special units of the police participated in the military actions in Kijevo, in Drnis, in Sibenik; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special police units did not even exist in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina at that time. These special police units came into existence on the 28th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's put aside special police units. The police participated in the military actions in Kijevo, in Drnis, in Sibenik with the JNA and the Territorial Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police only participated in defending the area at the Miljevacki plateau in June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, were you present at the 16th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was held in Banja Luka on the 12th of May, 1992? Do you remember that? Were you present for that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not attend that session, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you attend -- do you remember attending any kind of a session in Banja Luka, any kind of event where Ratko Mladic spoke and attending it with Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I attended the one session. Whether it was in Novi Grad, and another meeting which also took place in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I cannot remember -- I cannot remember having attended the one in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The ones you remember attending, did they occur in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: May, May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that with precision. I wish I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, do you remember --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe the one in Novi Grad was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember Ratko Mladic speaking?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ratko Mladic is a good orator. He spoke at all the sessions of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska when he was invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, by the way, why were you at these sessions? What was the reason for you to be at these sessions?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the session which was held at Novi Grad, it was a debate between two Assemblies, that of the Republika Srpska and the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, about some issues of unification. I hail from Novi Grad, and the representatives of the area asked me to attend the session, and I attended just a part of one session to discuss that particular issue. And I didn't stay throughout these sessions because I had to go back on account of my previous commitments, official duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In May of 1992, you were a colonel; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992 I was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there any other Colonel Djukic in the 9th Corps?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another Djukic, but he was not a colonel. He was a Captain First Class Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So there was no other Colonel Djukic in the 9th Corps?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 19th of May, 1992, there were no colonels by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So you're the only Colonel Djukic in the 9th Corps until that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute. On page 64, line 19, the question is put: "In May of 1992, you were a colonel; correct?" "Yes, in 1992 I was a colonel." Now, line -- just a second, just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now you say in line 25: "Until the 19th of May, 1992, there were no colonels by that time -- oh, there were no colonels by that name." I'm sorry. By which name, Djukic? But you were a colonel already by May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was Colonel Djukic in the 9th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you were a colonel in the 9th Corps in May of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was a colonel in 1992 until the 18th of July, 1992, when I was promoted to the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Therefore, it is not correct to say that in May of 1992 there were no colonels by the name of Djukic in the 9th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not what I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, look at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said the only colonel was Borislav Djukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you look at line 25 of page 64 it says: "Until the 19th of May, 1992, there were no colonels by that name." Which name? The question had been: "So there was no other Colonel Djukic in the 9th Corps." Now, you're saying there were -- by the 19th of May, 1992, there was no colonel by the name of Djukic in the 9th Corps. But you say in May you were a colonel and you are Djukic. Now, one of the two must be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, interpreter's note: I added "by that name," because that's the way I understood the witness to have said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were the colonels on the territory of Croatia until the 19th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand this last sentence. Even if the interpreter added "by that name," it -- my question would still stand, because then it would say: There was no colonel by that day, but he was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you -- or did you mean to say there were no other colonels, other than yourself? Is that what you said or you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not the only colonel. There were a number of colonels, but I was Colonel Borislav Djukic in the month of May 1992. There were more Djukics but they were not colonels. There was Captain First Class Djukic, lieutenant-colonels, and majors also, but the only colonel was me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have Exhibit 45, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this is the minutes from the 16th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina held in Banja Luka on the 12th of May, 1992. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We need the English on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could turn, please, to -- I'll wait for the English. There we go. If we could turn, please, in the English to 3537 and in the B/C/S 7740.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you'll see that in these minutes there's a -- Ratko Mladic speaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, please, in the B/C/S -- and actually, the next page in English, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you see -- it says Ratko Mladic's speech. And if you look -- if we could go to the bottom of the page we're on in B/C/S. And in the English I'm focussed on the top of the page that is showing which is 3538. And he says -- Mr. Mladic says: "Martic is here. I do not point this out because I want to take credit for the results but because he was my witness. But to the left of him are Colonel Djukic and Colonel Spanovic." Now, that's you, isn't it, sir? You were there with Mr. Mladic and Mr. Spanovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's -- I don't want to argue about where it was. The minutes say where it was. But do you remember this now? And that is you that's being referred to; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that this might be Colonel Djordje Djukic, a member of the Army of the Republika Srpska, who was later promoted to general and was assistant for logistics at the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He wasn't -- he wasn't in the 9th Corps, was he?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djordje Djukic was not in the 9th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at -- if we could, let's look at in the English, a little later in the speech, 3542, and in the B/C/S 7745. And if we could look at the top of the page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you -- and I'm looking at the middle of the page in the English. He says -- do you see this where he says: "Djukic and Spanovic are here also. Spanovic came later. Djukic knows what the strength of the Knin Corps was at the time, when following an order I received by phone I reached the decision to move for the coastal rim." Now, sir, he's talking about you, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What page is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's in the middle of the page 3542, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 3542. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He's talking about you, isn't he, Mr. Djukic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now if we could look, please, at another part of the speech. It's at 3348 in the English and 7749 in the B/C/S. Wait a minute. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I think I meant 3548 in the English. Yes, I'm sorry, I meant 3548 in the English and 7749 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And at the -- towards the bottom of the page in the English, and I'm not exactly sure where it is on the B/C/S, so you'll just have to look for it. And maybe if we could show the whole -- if we're able to show the whole page. It's a little hard to read, I know. But he says -- this is still Mladic speaking. He says: "The Knin Corps was successful because under a single command in the zone of the corps were the JNA, the Territorial Defence forces, and Martic's police. Isn't that right, Martic? And because he and I -- I call him and say: Give me 40 policemen here at Kijevo and you took part in the fighting. Isn't that right, Milan?" Do you see that part of the text, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's -- must be towards the bottom, I think. It actually may be on the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You should find it. It's after the sentence with: "Thousand commanders in one zone."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it -- I believe it's on the next page. I apologise. It looks to me like it's on the next page. Of the B/C/S. Yes. Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. It is there on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you now see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But do you see it? The question was: Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it this Kalinovik? Went to find Kalinovik --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... he says: It's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, no, no, it's there. It's on the screen. I'm almost certain it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It says: "The Knin Corps was successful because under a single command in the zone of the corps were the JNA, the Territorial Defence forces, and Martic's police. Isn't that right, Martic?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And he specifically talks about 40 police taking part in the fighting in Kijevo and that Milan Martic did as well. Do you see that? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that's how it was. The police -- the police participated in these actions within the 9th Corps along with the JNA and the TO, exactly as Mr. Mladic said; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Mladic knows more about this than I, and I think he's the one you should be asking the question. I was on the left wing. I headed for that church, what we said yesterday, and then I continued on to Vrlika. Afterwards, when the siege of Kijevo was lifted and the road was open, I know that the SAO Krajina police entered. And that evening I saw Minister Martic on TV and some other familiar faces taking down the plaque on the building of the Kijevo police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What -- by the way --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was surprised by the fact that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did the plaque say, by the way, that they took down?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Kijevo police station." I think that's what it said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of Croatia, the usual sort of thing, and then Kijevo police station. And there was the flag of the Republic of Croatia, too. They called it the chequer-board. I know because I had been to that station several times for negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- so as I understand your answer now, the police could have participated in the action without you knowing about it, which is why you said we should ask Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the conditions of warfare that prevailed and since there was a siege to be lifted, normally after JNA units had passed through, police units are found entering the area to restore order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay, but that wasn't the question. The question was: The -- as I understand your testimony, the police couldn't have participated in the fighting without you knowing about it. Because you said you did this one flank, you were on the left wing, and we should ask Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it like that. I said that you should ask Ratko Mladic about possible police involvement, whether they were involved at all, or perhaps whether the police came after the road had been cleared and arrived at that police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I take it you're telling us we should ask Ratko Mladic because you do not know yourself for sure; that's why?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly can't answer along my axis, along the axis along which I commanded my unit there were no police of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. There were no members of the police there. Kijevo was not under my command; it was under the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was several units involved and not just my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's talk about Kijevo. You may have said this already, but let's just be clear about it. Kijevo was a Croatian village, inhabited by Croats in 1991, in August of 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it was -- on both sides of Kijevo were Croatian villages; correct -- I mean Serbian villages, villages that were inhabited by Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the Knin-Sinj or Vrlika-Sinj road, in front of Kijevo and behind Kijevo there were Serb villages, but on both flanks there were Croat villages, on the left and on the right, the village of Maovica and the village of Levestice [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But along the road, along the road that you spoke about there were Serb villages on each side of Kijevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front and behind, which means in front and behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, in fact, Kijevo was cut off and blockaded by the Serb villages. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely. Kijevo still had a way out. On the left and on the right, there were no Croat villages. And let me tell you this: Between the 24th and the 25th the commander of the police station, Ivica Bucic, organised the evacuation of everyone from the village of Kijevo across Kozjak to the village of Maovica and then on to Sinj and Drnis. The entire population was in fact evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, not the entire population, because there was still people there when you attacked on the on the 26th of August, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We deblocked the village of Kijevo. There were still some locals there, and they stayed there. And for a while, while I was holding the area, I provided their supplies, their medical supplies, their water, their food --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, please. Now, you told us a story about the body of Dusan Vranjes that was blocked from going from Drnis to the village of Cetina. And you said that it couldn't go -- it went to Knin and then it couldn't go to Cetina because it was blocked by Kijevo. Correct? Do you remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that's not what I said. I said Vranjes had been killed at the Sibenik police station. And the Kijevo police station did not allow for his body to pass through the village of Kijevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And his body was coming from?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and then all the people assembled --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please listen to my question. His body -- you said his body was travelling from Drnis to Knin and then it was going to go through Kijevo to Cetina.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Sibenik across Drnis to Knin, for him to be buried in his native village of Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in fact it's possible -- you can go from Drnis to Cetina without going through Kijevo; isn't that right? You go to Drnis, then you go to Miocic, to Vrlika, to Civljani, to Cetnia, without going through Kijevo. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. It's most certainly not correct. If you fly, yes, perhaps, but there is no land road from Drnis leading to Cetina. There is only this one road, and there is the other road that was open was across Mount Svilaja, but that is far away, and nobody ever takes that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you say -- you say -- I'm looking at page 32 of Exhibit 23. You say that there is no road that goes from Drnis -- no, I'm sorry, did I say 32? I meant page 31, I'm sorry. There's no road that goes from Drnis to Miocic to Vrlika to Civljani to Cetina?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you there's the main road from Drnis across Knin, and then there's the long way around leading through the village of Maovica and then it goes down to Vrlika and then you go to Gornje Civljani and then on to Cetina. However, the village of Maovica was blocked too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was blocking that road, blocking it there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Maovica at the time, and you can go back to a document of the commander of the 9th Corps 1-4, the 5th of April, 1991, there was a parapolice unit there numbering between 150 and 20 members that was deployed in that particular village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk -- let's get back to Kijevo. You testified that there were hundreds of police in Kijevo, and I think -- I wasn't absolutely sure about this, but I think you may have even suggested that there were between 1.000 and 1500 armed men in Kijevo in August of 1991 because you said that the number of the army corresponded to the number of the residents of Kijevo. Is that really your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I testified as follows. That spring in Kijevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the Kijevo police station was set up and it numbered 50 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you because you don't need to repeat all your testimony. My only question is: Is it your testimony that there were between 1.000 and 1500 armed men in Kijevo in August of 1991, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My testimony is there was gradual reinforcements to those forces there. Eventually about 1.000 men were stationed at Kijevo, including both MUP and the Kijevo volunteer detachment --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and they organised attacks, launched attacks, against the buffer zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, that is a gross exaggeration, isn't it? There were, at most, 40 to 50 policemen in Kijevo when you attacked it on the 26th of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, allow me to again produce the particular piece of evidence that I have been referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, just answer my question, please. There were not 1.000 --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative. The answer to your question is negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 1.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get back to that -- that figure in a moment. You also testified that what caused the attack on the 26th of August, 1991, was attacks by Croats on the buffer zone on the 25th of August, 1991. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. On the 25th of August, the morning of the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I take it that this was one of the -- this is an important fact, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I take it this is something that you -- you -- this is one of the things that you told Mr. Nikolic about back when you met him in 2004. You told us -- you told him about all the important events, and this would have been one of them; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for Your Honours' benefit, I put that question to the witness because of course this is an event which was not put to any of our witnesses who testified about Kijevo, including, in particular, Witness MM-078. In fact, this is the first time that we have heard about any such attack on the 25th of August, 1991. So -- anyhow, that's for Your Honours' benefit. I'll go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, sir, the attack on Kijevo was planned before that happened on the 25th of August, 1991, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that we're talking about lifting the siege off the Kijevo road, but that wasn't planned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's -- sir, let's --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the lifting of the blockade had been provoked by an attack by those forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at Exhibit 212 in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we done with Mladic's speech?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it is in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is. It is Exhibit 45, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is -- Exhibit 212 is an ultimatum that's dated the 18th of August, 1991, and it's from Milan Martic. You're familiar with this document, right, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're not -- you were not -- you were not aware that on the 18th of August, 1991, Milan Martic issued this ultimatum concerning the police station in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those days there were things being said on Radio Knin about an ultimatum that was sent to the Kijevo police station. Now, whether this ultimatum had been sent by Martic and/or Babic, or both of them jointly, this is not something that I can say. However, this document, this ultimatum, probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's look at the second page of -- if this has a second page, or if we scroll down to the bottom in the B/C/S. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does that answer your question about who sent it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Milan Martic" here, but let me tell you something: This is just not his signature at all. Get one of the official documents. I have never seen Milan Martic's signature look anything resembling this. Milan Martic usually puts two Ms there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this document has been -- is in evidence in our case, and it has never been disputed that this ultimatum was issued by Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So anyhow, if we could go to the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is, in fact, what the attack on Kijevo was all about on the 26th of August, 1991, isn't it, sir? Milan Martic says in the second paragraph: "You have a police station in the village of Kijevo in Knin municipality. This ultimatum is to warn you that our forces will attack this police station at a time we find appropriate if your police forces do not withdraw from this village within 48 hours from the moment of receipt of this ultimatum." And eight days later, that's exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a question I must ask. Why, then, did Martic not attack Kijevo on the 20th, as stated in the ultimatum? It was right there, the buffer zone, and he couldn't have possibly attacked Kijevo across our lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, the attack occurred on the 26th of August, for whatever reason, and Milan Martic was -- participated in the attack and the -- and in fact, he -- as you say, he went to the police station and was there when the sign on the police station was torn down; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the time that elapsed between these two ultimata was used to allow the situation to die down a little. I can tell you that we even had meetings with generals from the General Staff and ministers from the Yugoslav army who were there who attended these talks and who talked to the leaders, even the political leaders of the area, as well as the police leaders. I remember this one particular talk with the chief of the police administration from Split attending, Nikola --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you. I want to stay focussed on the issue here. And the -- the attack on Kijevo was about the police station in Kijevo, wasn't it, just as the ultimatum says?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, when the buffer zones were violated and attacked, an assignment was received and the lifting of the siege was carried out under the command of the corps commander. The station happened to be right in the middle of the village of Kijevo, and it was from that station that an attack was launched against members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was from the police station in Vrlika that an attack was launched against other members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, do you find it odd that this ultimatum that's issued on the 18th of August, 1991, doesn't say anything about 1.000 armed men being in Kijevo, it doesn't say anything about blockades preventing Serb villages from being replenished, it doesn't say anything about any of those things. All it talks about is the police station in the village of Kijevo. Does that strike you as odd?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as I said, I've never seen this document before, never clapped eyes on it. I'm entirely unfamiliar with its substance. I heard over the radio that there was some sort of ultimatum being issued but, as you say, 48 hours had elapsed, and by the 12th nothing whatsoever had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you can read the document, it's very short. You can see there's nothing about 1.000 armed men in Kijevo, there's nothing about blockades preventing Serb villages from getting food or -- there's nothing about that, right? You agree with me? There's nothing about that in the ultimatum. And my question is: Does that surprise you, since those seem to be the major issues that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly didn't produce this document. If I had been the one, if I had been the one issuing an ultimatum like that, this document would have looked very different. I can assure you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just say to you, sir, that you -- I hear you saying at the end of the 48 hours the attack was not launched, it was launched later. But you'll see that where the sentence about the 48 hours appears it says that: "We shall attack the police station at that time we find appropriate," not on expiry of the 48 hours. Okay? Just bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the attack. The attack, just so we're clear, occurred on the 26th of August and was over in a matter of hours; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lifting of the siege took three or four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On the 26th of August? It was on the 26th of August; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you testified that you -- you testified that you used a pincer movement and that the plan was "brilliantly planned and executed." Now, who planned the attack?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no plan for this attack at all. How many times have I repeated this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, but -- sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any sort of plan for an attack --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said it was brilliantly planned. Those are your words, it was brilliantly planned. So my question is: Who planned it? Was it you? Was it somebody else?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the lifting of the siege was brilliantly carried out. So, please, the lifting of the siege was brilliantly carried out. All casualties were avoided. There were casualties on neither side. The lifting of the siege was planned when these acts of provocation were carried out and when the buffer zones were violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There was -- there was a plan for the attack before the attack occurred; correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no plan of attack. No attack was ever planned against the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think maybe we're misunderstanding each other. All I mean is that before the morning of the 26th of August, 1991, before the JNA and the TO and maybe the police started moving towards Kijevo, there was some plan. Somebody said: You're going to go there, and you're going to go there, and you move in that direction, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have that kind of plan. We did not plan to lift the siege of Kijevo and the police station at all. Beforehand we had agreed with the police for the JNA to secure buses for the police station, based on an agreement between the authorities in Zagreb and the Military Naval District for the police station to be relocated to Sinj for tensions to dwindle. The corps commander even sent the vehicles there, and it was due to pure luck and the good reasoning of the commander of the police station that no clashes erupted; rather, the vehicles were pulled out and sent back to the corps command, the barracks. So our thinking was we had to execute this design agreed by the leaders, by the authorities. It wasn't like we were planning an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try and move on. You said that there was a pincer movement, so the -- the attack came from at least two directions; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military terms a pincer movement is something you do from one side. When you are surrounding someone, you surround them on all sides, just for the sake of clarity. The lifting of the siege was carried out from one side only, and the units in my command were in charge of the left side of the pincer movement in relation to the Knin-Vrlika-Sinj road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And there was some units that were responsible for the right side of the pincer movement; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because the right side -- there was a steeply rising slope there with an elevation called Kozjak, the peak, it's called Bat, and there was no way the soldiers could have gone there. And this area was of no interest at all to us. We would have gained nothing by going there. We would have just wasted some of our manpower. So we didn't do the right side of the pincer, if that's what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you did say that this plan was brilliantly planned and executed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: "This plan," can we clarify what is it when he, in fact, said, was brilliantly -- "this action," he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "This action," I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: "This action was brilliantly planned and executed." This is yesterday, page 40, line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's 9749, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What he means by "this action was brilliantly planned." Maybe we can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask a different question about it, but perhaps it will clarify it in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I interrupted you only because you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I said "the plan," yes, instead of the action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You said something about this or so, and what was at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, you're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So this was then more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that the action was brilliantly planned and executed. And you've told us that there were at least 1.000 armed men in Kijevo, but you captured only 60 MUP officers. I guess the obvious question is: Where did everyone else go?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I didn't say at all that it was brilliantly planned or devised. What I said was that the lifting of the siege was brilliantly executed or carried out. And what I had in mind is if you have a siege like that being lifted with no casualties at all, not on the JNA side, not on the enemy side, not a single civilian was killed. Nobody at all was wounded. And now you're taking it back to this --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, let's put aside the brilliant --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me to finish your answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, you've explained --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to tell you about the thousand --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that I do want to know about.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't tell you about the thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have an operation being carried out -- say, for example, the Normandy landings. Not all the German forces were captured in Normandy. It was just part of their forces. And the rest pulled out exactly along these very same roads on their way to Germany back in World War II. Likewise, these forces had two different roads to beat the retreat. Some of them crossed this mountain, the feature, the one known as Kozjak, all the way to the village of Maovica, and then from there on to Vrlika and Sinj with the remaining forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, how can you describe the action as having been brilliantly executed when 940 armed men escaped to fight another day? How can you say that's brilliantly executed when you captured 60 out of a thousand armed men?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, for me what constitutes brilliance is when you lift a siege without sustaining a single casualty or inflicting any casualties at all on your enemy. That, for me, is top-notch, both in terms of my evidence here and my opinions as an ordinary human being. I am indeed very happy that it was done the way it was done and that there were no casualties to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The truth is, sir, that there were not a thousand men in that village. There were -- there were 50 or 60 MUP officers, and you captured them. That's the truth, isn't it, sir? And that's why there were no casualties and that's why you captured 60.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that is certainly not a fact. I regret not having lists of members of the volunteer units on me right now with their full names with the numbers of each single rifle that they had signed for. This is what we captured. This is what we forwarded to the corps command, and they in turn forwarded this and all the other commands to the General Staff of the JNA. I would, indeed, be a happy man to have those documents available to me so that I could show you so you can see for yourself exactly how many men were actually there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, we don't have those, sir. Let's talk about the -- how the attack was conducted. You -- in fact, houses in Kijevo were deliberately set fire to and looted. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the lifting of the siege, not a single house was set fire to, not a single house was looted. There may have been damage to some houses, houses from which we had been fired at --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and these houses were damaged by the firing opened by units involved in lifting the siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you explain then how it is that if the action was finished on the 26th of August, 1991, there were houses that were set fire to the next day, on the 27th of August, 1991? How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of August, the JNA units were not in Kijevo. On the 27th of August, the JNA units were near Vrlika. The JNA units -- please, continued their operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... who was in Kijevo on the 27th of August, it was the TO and the police; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure. I do assume that these could have been police units, not TO units. These could have been looters and fire-starters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's talk about the church. The church was, in fact, damaged during the attack on the 26th of August, 1991, that's damaged; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, to some extent window-panes had been shattered, I know about that, and the houses sustained several hits by mortars and perhaps tanks, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Not the houses, the church --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the church was not damaged because the church is built of stone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The church was hit by at least seven projectiles, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hardly tell you whether it was one, five, or seven hits. If it was fired at at all, I suppose some sort of missile was used, but my order was clear: The church was not to be destroyed, and indeed the church was not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not talking about destroyed. It was -- will you accept -- will you agree or do you not know that it was hit by seven -- at least seven projectiles?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that at this moment. It is possible. It may have been hit because up on the spire of the church there was a machine-gun nest and there were also rifle positions of the MUP on the church itself, on the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
